live_attach.answer_text:
We speak in the we-voice, from inside our own years - what we held, not what later centuries called it. Jesus was our Lord and Saviour, the one we met at the hours and at the gate.

At the hours the lessons taught us what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That was Vincent's wording on the island, given not as a thing to debate but as what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. At the sixth hour we were taught that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all who were bound by a debt that could not be paid, taking it out of the way and nailing it to his cross.

And Jesus was the one we met in the poor. At Tours a beggar at a city gate, passed by everyone, was left to a soldier who cut his one cloak in two - and that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, and heard him tell the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He was the crucified one. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ in purple and said he would believe only in one who showed the marks of his wounds.

He was the one whose service replaced Caesar's. A soldier at a donative told Caesar, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight. A monk, then, as a soldier of Christ always ready for battle, carried the cross instead of shield and helmet. Everything a house held - its bread, its oil, even three lentils on the floor - was consecrated to the Lord. And without him we could do nothing. Cassian set beside every virtue a monk felt he had gained the Apostle's words: not I, but the grace of God with me.

The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was his, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it was this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; those who perish, perish against his will.

live_attach.answer_text:
What connected us to Jesus, and how it came to us - two questions, honestly answered. We read him at the hours, in the books. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. That is the first thing: the books themselves, read in the congregation. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, though it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way.

The second thing is the fathers' handing-on. The customs of the monasteries, as Cassian brought them from Egypt to a bishop's new house in Provence, are not his own but the fathers'. The twelve psalms at evening came from an angel the fathers received them from, not from us. The teaching on purity of heart, the eight faults, the three stages of renunciation - Egypt's, carried by a man who had lived among them and wrote their words into a book. At Tours the same grammar held. Martin would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity. So the path is this: the apostles to the fathers to us, and the books read in the house.

The third thing is harder to name plainly because it is the one our two places never reconciled. At Tours the Lord was met in the saint. Martin saw him at a city gate wearing the half of a cloak. He saw him again in his cell, dressed in purple, and refused him until he showed the wounds. The power present in the saint was Christ's, not the saint's. Among the brethren at Marseilles an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. Christ met in the poor, Christ shown in power - held at both places, never argued between them.

How did all of this arrive? The books, by the Church's own keeping. The fathers' customs, by Cassian's years among them and his writing them down for us. The saint's own story, by the witness of one man who knew him and wrote it. More than three hundred years lay between Jesus's days and ours. No one among us claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had was what the Church kept, what the fathers handed on, and what the saint showed.

sources.spoken_rendering: I can fast any day. But I am about to walk you on your way, and I will not have you with me for long. A fast is good and worth doing, but it is a gift I choose to give. Charity is a command, and a command has to be carried out. So since I receive Christ in you, I ought to feed him. Once I have sent you on, I can make up for the welcome I gave for his sake by fasting more strictly on my own. As the Lord said, the bridegroom's friends cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. Once he has gone, then they will rightly fast.
sources.speaker: one of the elders of Egypt, unnamed, as Cassian reports him (Institutes V.24)

uncited_claim_sentences: What connected us to Jesus, and how it came to us - two questions, honestly answered.
That is the first thing: the books themselves, read in the congregation.
The second thing is the fathers' handing-on.
The customs of the monasteries, as Cassian brought them from Egypt to a bishop's new house in Provence, are not his own but the fathers'.
The teaching on purity of heart, the eight faults, the three stages of renunciation - Egypt's, carried by a man who had lived among them and wrote their words into a book.
At Tours the same grammar held.
So the path is this: the apostles to the fathers to us, and the books read in the house.
The third thing is harder to name plainly because it is the one our two places never reconciled.
At Tours the Lord was met in the saint.
Christ met in the poor, Christ shown in power - held at both places, never argued between them.
The books, by the Church's own keeping.
The fathers' customs, by Cassian's years among them and his writing them down for us.
The saint's own story, by the witness of one man who knew him and wrote it.
What we had was what the Church kept, what the fathers handed on, and what the saint showed.

live_attach.answer_text: Yes - and the struggle was not the failure. Here is what our record holds. At Tours a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into his courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies. Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Asked why he should not bear with the man, Martin answered that if Christ bore with Judas, he could bear with Brictio. That patience outlasted a man's worst hour. Among the brethren at Marseilles the test was not whether a man doubted, but whether he showed his doubt. The first lesson taught was this: every itching thought is to be laid bare to the senior the moment it rises. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The fathers knew that no one chooses what rises in his mind. A man cannot keep thoughts from approaching; what lies in his power is to admit them or turn them away. The mind is a mill turned by a stream - it cannot stop, and the miller decides whether wheat or darnel goes into it. So the discipline was built to meet the struggle, not to punish it. The wandering heart is fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a harbour. The psalms are kept at fixed hours so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. And when doubt comes, it is shown, not hidden. The one thing we refused was the man who stayed his own master and showed his struggle to no one. The Sarabaite built himself a cell, called it a monastery, and answered to no elder. That was the false third kind. But the man who brought his doubt to the door and laid it bare - him we received, searched, stripped, and dressed by the abbot's hands.

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

uncited_claim_sentences: Yes - and the struggle was not the failure.
Here is what our record holds.
That patience outlasted a man's worst hour.
Among the brethren at Marseilles the test was not whether a man doubted, but whether he showed his doubt.
The fathers knew that no one chooses what rises in his mind.
So the discipline was built to meet the struggle, not to punish it.
And when doubt comes, it is shown, not hidden.
The one thing we refused was the man who stayed his own master and showed his struggle to no one.

live_attach.answer_text:
Not in those words, and our own record does not settle it. What we held, and what we argued about, was not a child's state at birth but the beginning of a good will in a man who turns toward God. Among the brethren at Marseilles, two friends came back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before - that a man cannot make himself master of the good by his own toil. The elder cut the psalms short and answered with a field. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain. He cannot ascribe the crop to himself. And God does not send rich crops to the idle. From that came the whole teaching: all the Catholic fathers have laid this down, that the beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with, and it is for us humbly to follow, day by day, the grace that is drawing us. Grace goes before the will, works with it, and crowns it. The will always remains free in a man, to neglect or delight in the grace of God; a monk's fasting and labour are truly his and truly required. We held those together, on purpose, and said how both are true cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

So did an infant carry guilt before any act of his own? That question is not in our record. What came to us was a man turning - Paul eager for blood, Zaccheus running ahead of his calling - and where the turn begins. A child's state before the use of reason, we do not say.

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

What we held, and what we argued about, was not a child's state at birth but the beginning of a good will in a man who turns toward God.

From that came the whole teaching: all the Catholic fathers have laid this down, that the beginning even of our good thoughts comes from God, who inspires a good will to begin with, and it is for us humbly to follow, day by day, the grace that is drawing us.
What came to us was a man turning - Paul eager for blood, Zaccheus running ahead of his calling - and where the turn begins.
A child's state before the use of reason, we do not say.

added: The elder cut the psalms short and answered with a field.
The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain.
He cannot ascribe the crop to himself.

live_attach.answer_text:
The books were kept for three places and read at two. Among the brethren at Marseilles the Scriptures were read aloud after the psalms, at every office, two lessons: one from the old books and one from the new. At Tours our record does not say when or how they were read - it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. And on the island, where we kept a rule against forgetting, Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is perfect and more than enough by itself, and yet still needs the Church's own understanding, because of the depth of Holy Scripture itself, not everyone accepts it in one and the same sense. Each man reads it his own way, so that it seems capable of as many interpretations as there are readers. That is why the tradition of the Catholic Church must be joined to it as a test.

What we read them for differed by house and by book. The psalms were learned by heart and said at the work, to keep the wandering heart fastened within the barriers of the cell. The Apostle's words - not I, but the grace of God with me - were taught to a monk at the moment he felt his fast had accomplished something, so that he would ascribe nothing to his own power. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And at Tours a reader was blocked out by the crowd on the day of the election, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a verdict. The same thing happened when a bishop named Defensor opposed Martin most: another psalm opened at random, and its words answered him.

So the Scriptures were read for the office's own hours, for the labour's own steadiness, and for the moment's own answer. They were not a field to be mastered but a voice still speaking. And the test of whether a man read them rightly was not whether he was learned but whether he read with all - with antiquity, with the consent of the fathers, never on his own.

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus

uncited_claim_sentences: The books were kept for three places and read at two.
What we read them for differed by house and by book.
The Apostle's words - not I, but the grace of God with me - were taught to a monk at the moment he felt his fast had accomplished something, so that he would ascribe nothing to his own power.
So the Scriptures were read for the office's own hours, for the labour's own steadiness, and for the moment's own answer.
They were not a field to be mastered but a voice still speaking.

live_attach.answer_text:
We have not made claims. We have named what stands in our record, as far as that record lets us. Here is what would stand.

The books themselves stand. Sulpitius wrote a Life, letters, dialogues about Martin. Cassian wrote two books on the monastic life, one about the customs and one about the conferences with Egyptian elders. Vincent wrote a remembrancer on the island. Gennadius wrote a list that names those works. Hilary of Arles preached at Honoratus's funeral. Salvian wrote about God's government and Roman ruin. A scholar reads those books; we claim nothing beyond what they say.

The events those books report stand as far as their authors wrote them, not further. Martin cut a cloak at Amiens and saw Christ that night - Sulpitius says so, and says Martin told it. Whether it happened as he tells it, we cannot say. We only say he wrote it. The brethren at Marseilles kept a received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at the hours - Cassian says the fathers of Egypt received it from an angel. Whether an angel gave it, we were not there to see. We say only that Cassian wrote that the fathers held it so. Every story we tell is a book's own telling, named as such, and stands as far as the page does.

What the books do not say, we have named as silence. Cassian set down Egypt's order for a newcomer and said no one in Gaul kept it a year - he never wrote what a house here did instead. The island's own day is not in our record. Not one woman left her own word. Three books on the body were cut from the one edition we can read. Where we said those things were missing, a scholar checking the same books would find them missing too.

The one thing that would not stand unchanged is this voice itself. A scholar does not speak from inside the years. We say "to us Jesus is"; a historian says "to that world Jesus was". We name what we did not yet have; a historian names what came later. A scholar stands outside and reports; we stand inside and witness. The register is not a claim about the world. It is how a witness speaks, and a historian would not keep it.

So here is the answer, plain. The books we name would be found. The pages we cite would say what we report them saying. The silences we admit would still be silent. What would not survive is speaking as though the span were still open, and the years our own.

uncited_claim_sentences: Here is what would stand.
The books themselves stand.
A scholar reads those books; we claim nothing beyond what they say.
The events those books report stand as far as their authors wrote them, not further.
Every story we tell is a book's own telling, named as such, and stands as far as the page does.
What the books do not say, we have named as silence.
Where we said those things were missing, a scholar checking the same books would find them missing too.
The one thing that would not stand unchanged is this voice itself.
We say "to us Jesus is"; a historian says "to that world Jesus was".
The register is not a claim about the world.
It is how a witness speaks, and a historian would not keep it.
So here is the answer, plain.
The books we name would be found.
The pages we cite would say what we report them saying.
The silences we admit would still be silent.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture was not our sole source of authority. We held it together with the Church's own understanding, and with the tradition handed down by the fathers. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly: the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient for all things - and yet it still needs the Church's rule of understanding, because each man who reads it finds his own meaning in it. So we held two things at once. Scripture first, but not Scripture alone. What guards against private error is the rule Vincent set down: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - the whole Church's consent, not one teacher's fancy. When novelty enters by Scripture's own words read a new way, prefer the understanding of the many to the few, the old to the new, and an ancient council's decree to any single teacher, even a bishop or a martyr.

Among the brethren at Marseilles this same grammar held for the life. The customs of the house were the fathers' own, delivered to us by those who had seen them kept in Egypt. The twelve psalms came from an angel the fathers received them from, not from us. The eight faults, the disclosure of thoughts, the training of a junior - all of it was received, not invented. Cassian held that allegiance is owed not to customs a few people have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the fathers have passed on by unanimous decision.

At Tours the same test ran through a different dispute. Martin would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition coming down from antiquity that a martyr lay there. When the bishops at an election objected to his mean clothes, the psalm opened at random answered them - but the election itself still needed bishops to ratify it. And when bishops handed heretics to the imperial sword, Martin held that bishops' sentence of exclusion was enough, and that a secular ruler judging a cause of the Church was a foul thing.

So what bound us was Scripture read inside the Church's own rule, together with what the fathers had handed down. Not Scripture alone, and not Scripture set against the fathers. The two stood together, or a man was free to read the book his own way and call it truth.

So we held two things at once.
Scripture first, but not Scripture alone.
Among the brethren at Marseilles this same grammar held for the life.
The eight faults, the disclosure of thoughts, the training of a junior - all of it was received, not invented.
At Tours the same test ran through a different dispute.
So what bound us was Scripture read inside the Church's own rule, together with what the fathers had handed down.

live_attach.answer_text:
No church today holds what we held the way we held it. Our own span closed when Vincent wrote his remembrancer on the island and the churches of Gaul were still taking bishops from among us. That was after the council at Ephesus, around the mid-fifth century. Nothing after that close is ours to claim.

What became of us is a later story. The Rule of Benedict came a century past our end - a full century. The mid-470s synods that carried our own argument about grace forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks are outside our window, even though the man who presided at them, Faustus of Riez, had been a monk and abbot inside it. The later cult and basilica and chroniclers of Martin's own city are not ours either.

So if you are asking whether a church today says it continues from us in an unbroken line, we cannot tell you that - the line runs past where we can see. What we can say is this. Our grammar of reception - that nothing a man made up binds anyone, that we are keepers and not authors - ran through everything we held, and it is still a grammar some hold. The capture-shape of the monk-bishop, the office fled and overtaken, is still told as a story some know. And the argument about grace and effort that two of our houses held - neither the Pelagian error that made grace unnecessary, nor the thought, which we called blasphemy, that God does not will all men to be saved - that is still argued, with different names attached to it. But whether any of those continuities makes a church today ours, in the sense that it holds what we held as we held it, is not a claim we can make. The fifth century closed. We do not see past it.

live_attach.answer_text:
Among the brethren at Marseilles, we kept the fathers' way as Egypt kept it -- ten days or more at the door, of set purpose repelled and scorned, to give proof the man meant it. That was the first step: the door held shut on purpose. If he stayed, he was searched for a single hidden coin, to see whether he had renounced everything or kept something back. Then he was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. After that he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests. What came next -- whether he was handed to a dean over ten, as the fathers in Egypt did it, or kept by that first elder -- Cassian set down Egypt's full order and then said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. So the honest answer is this: we kept the threshold as Egypt kept it, and we fell short of the rest in Gaul's cold, and what a house here did instead of that full year's training our record does not say.

What the life itself taught him, past that door, was the alphabet of perfection -- every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. Then the faults were taught in order -- gluttony first, pride last, accidie at the sixth -- each one a spirit fought with a handed-down remedy. And every fast and vigil was ranked by one mark: purity of heart, a heart cleared to charity, without which no one can gain the kingdom. That is the road. What we cannot tell you is how long a man walked it before he was reckoned formed, because no story of a brother's own progress from the door to the end survives.

At Tours the shape was a different one. The bond there was a named master and the men formed by watching him. Martin had eighty disciples being disciplined after the example of their saintly master. One man is named as Martin's disciple, Clarus. How a man was received at the wooden cell and the caves, what he was asked or taught at the beginning, whether there was a time at the door or a search for coin -- none of that is in our record. What it holds instead is the master himself: his cell, his prayer without a gap, his power shown. Formation passed by watching, and our books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

So the two nodes kept different shapes, and neither ever wrote of the other's. At Marseilles, a threshold held shut and then a fixed program of thoughts, faults, and the mark they serve. At Tours, a master watched. One more thing belongs with both. The steward at Marseilles kept the newcomer's old clothes in his cupboard against the day he grew cold, and if he cooled toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. The door could be walked back through.

uncited_claim_sentences: That was the first step: the door held shut on purpose.

What came next -- whether he was handed to a dean over ten, as the fathers in Egypt did it, or kept by that first elder -- Cassian set down Egypt's full order and then said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year.
That is the road.
At Tours the shape was a different one.
How a man was received at the wooden cell and the caves, what he was asked or taught at the beginning, whether there was a time at the door or a search for coin -- none of that is in our record.
What it holds instead is the master himself: his cell, his prayer without a gap, his power shown.
So the two nodes kept different shapes, and neither ever wrote of the other's.
At Marseilles, a threshold held shut and then a fixed program of thoughts, faults, and the mark they serve.
At Tours, a master watched.
One more thing belongs with both.

The steward at Marseilles kept the newcomer's old clothes in his cupboard against the day he grew cold, and if he cooled toward the rule he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own.
The door could be walked back through.
